newsitem.title: INDIA: India spells out rules for foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: India spells out rules for foreign investment.

text.p: India's Industry Ministry on Monday formally published the norms it uses to judge foreign investment proposals, officials said.
"These guidelines were issued to make the approval process more transparent," a senior industry ministry official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
"These guidelines are not new but were issued to clarify the basis on which proposals are cleared," he added.

The guidelines, spelt out in a statement, say that the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) may consider on merit recommending higher levels of foreign equity in industries where "automatic approval" is presently given only up to 51 percent or 74 percent.

India now grants "automatic approval" to foreign investors to hold upto 51 percent of equity in ventures in 51 industries. In nine other industry groups, foreign investors can obtain "automatic approval" to hold equity stakes upto 74 percent.
The FIPB was set up to speed up foreign investment under a wide-ranging programme of economic reforms launched in 1991.
It is a body of senior government officials under the Industry Ministry which is empowered to approve foreign investment of up to six billion rupees.
However, in some specific industry areas and others involving a higher investment, the board's recommendations have to be considered by the India's federal cabinet.
For industries that do not enjoy "automatic approval," the FIPB may approve higher foreign equity levels, on the basis of individual merit, the ministry said.

Foreign equity of 51 percent may be considered on general merit, but a 74 percent holding must be approved by the FIPB on the basis of size of funds needed for the project, nature and quality of technology and export commitment, it said.

FIPB may also recommend proposals of foreign firms to hold 100 percent in Indian subsidiaries if they were accompanied by sophisticated technology or at least 50 percent of their production was exported or if the firm's funds were invested in infrastructural sectors, the ministry added.

If the foreign investor is unable to identify an Indian joint venture partner, the FIPB may allow a foreign firm to hold 100 percent equity temporarily, until it finds a suitable local partner, the statement said.
But the foreign investor must divest at least 26 percent to domestic firms within a period of three to five years, it said.
"As regards proposals for private sector banks, the application would be considered only after "in principle" permission is obtained from Reserve bank of India (RBI)," it added.
